To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Schwann cells are a key component of the pathogenesis of diabetes-induced neuropathy.

Schwann cells are involved in the pathogenesis and progression of diabetic neuropathy and that disruption of the interactions of Schwann cells, neurons and microvessles contributes to the development of this condition.

Schwann cell interactions with microvessels and axons are disrupted in diabetic neuropathy; and these disruptions are associated with Schwann cell dysfunction, axonal degeneration and microvessel rarefaction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that Schwann cells play in the pathogenesis and progression of diabetic neuropathy.
the development of new treatments for diabetic neuropathy, with the ultimate aim of reducing its devastating impact on the lives of patients.
the development of novel therapies for diabetic neuropathy, which is one of the most common complications of diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Schwann cells are involved in diabetic neuropathy and the interactions of axons and microvasculature with Schwann cells are important in the pathogenesis.
diabetic neuropathy is not only a disorder of the axons and microvasculature, but also of Schwann cells.
the Schwann cells and the axon-microvessel unit are key players in the development and maintenance of diabetic neuropathy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Schwannopathy concept is a useful paradigm for understanding the pathogenesis of neuropathy in diabetes, but it is not the whole story.

the Schwann cells are the main cell type that are affected in diabetic neuropathy, which is characterized by the following: 1) Schwann cell death and dysfunction; 2) loss of axonal ensheathment; 3) Schwann cell dedifferentiation and proliferation; 4) impaired Schwann cell-axon and Schwann cell-vessel interactions.
Schwann cells are involved in the pathophysiology of diabetic neuropathy and that they play a role as a key regulator of the nerve environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that

diabetic neuropathy is a multifactorial disease that is not only caused by axonopathy but also by a combination of Schwannopathy and microangiopathy, which together lead to the loss of axonal function.

Schwann cell dysfunction is an important component of diabetic neuropathy and that targeting Schwann cell dysfunction might provide a therapeutic strategy to ameliorate the consequences of this disease.
Schwann cells are not passive bystanders in the development of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, but rather are actively involved in the disease process.
